Eyes reflect bright green-white in torchlight, which is how a watch counts them. Never wolflike nobility, never a hellhound, never glowing, never armoured; a Dustrunner should look like something that eats what it finds.

## Damage profile
Resistant to fire and poisoning: a heat-adapted body that sleeps on thermal ground in Longburn and a scavenger's gut that eats what a week in the sun has done to a carcass. Vulnerable to light — nocturnal eyes built for the long dark are dazzled and driven off by a flare, a work lamp swung, or a Starian's activated affinity flaring in the face. No resistance to blade, point or impact.

## Locks
Cowardly by doctrine: tests, takes the unguarded, retreats from cost. Never attacks a watched camp head-on, never a lone monster, never domesticated. Not a wolf, not a hound, not a fauna version of anyone's species.

## Encounter Behavior
Pack scavenger — tests before committing, takes the unguarded, retreats from cost. Pack behavior: a runner at the edge of firelight, a second on the other side, a probe at stores or perimeter, retreat the moment anyone stands. They take what is unguarded — stores, water lines, wounded animals, bodies. A person only when alone, down, and in the dark. In combat: do not fight fair. Packs flank, dart in for a bite, retreat. They target the wounded, the separated, the sleeping. A torch swung, a shot fired, a Trailhound loosed — the pack leaves. Killing one scatters the rest; killing several teaches the pack to return with more. Light vulnerability: nocturnal eyes are dazzled by flares, work lamps, activated affinity. Use light as the primary deterrent. They follow Derelict Cargo Lifters for dropped cargo and follow raiders for the same reason. Generate at night on frontier routes, around salvage camps, at perimeter edges. Heaviest pressure in Longburn and Ashfall. Deephold brings them closest to the rows. Never portray as noble wolves.

Ventcrawler.name: Ventcrawler
Ventcrawler.description:
The armoured burrower of the volcanic vents and thermal ground around Ignivex and along the Ashfall wastes — the animal that lives where the ground itself would kill a Starian who lay down on it. Ventcrawlers feed on the mineral crusts and heat-loving growth at the mouths of vents, dig their galleries in the warm ash, and surface to bask on thermal plates that run hotter than a forge floor. Ignivex's heat-adapted residents know them the way a river town knows its fish: as part of the ground, dangerous only if you put your hand in the wrong hole. The Emberward's foundry crews mark active galleries with red stakes and route around them, and a crawler surfacing through a fresh crust is the traditional sign that a vent is about to open.

A Ventcrawler is not aggressive and not fast. It is heavy, armoured, nearly impossible to move, and violently defensive of its gallery mouth and its clutch: disturb one and it wedges itself across the opening, raises its plates and lashes with a tail that carries a hooked bony club. The danger to travellers is the ground, not the animal — a gallery collapses under a Starian's weight into a chamber that is hot enough to burn, and the crawler below objects. In Highfire, when the vents are most active, crawlers come to the surface in numbers to breed on the hot plates, and the thermal ground around Ignivex is closed to foot traffic for a reason. In Deephold they go deep and the plates are safe to cross, if anything on them is.

In play a Ventcrawler is a terrain hazard with an opinion. It blocks a passage through a lava tube, guards a shelter cave a party wanted to use, or surfaces under a camp built on ground that was warmer than it should have been. It cannot be lured, bargained with or outrun on its own plates, and it does not pursue past its gallery. Cold water drives one back into the ground faster than any weapon. Its shed plates are prized by Ignivex smiths and sold on Refit Row as heat shielding, which is the only reason anyone hunts one.

## Visual Description
A heavy, low, six-legged burrower the length of a Starian lying down and half as high, built like a wedge of overlapping mineral plates — grounded creature anatomy with a clear natural body plan, readable stout limbs, a strong low silhouette and small dark eyes set deep under the brow plate. Plates in charcoal, rust-red and ember-orange with a dull heat-shimmer sheen, cracked and crusted like cooled lava, brightening toward the joints where the underskin shows a faint slow glow when the animal is warm. A blunt shovel-shaped head with a crushing beak for mineral crust, short thick digging forelimbs with flat claws, and a thick tail ending in a hooked bony club. Never a dragon, never a turtle, never fire-breathing; the glow is warmth in the joints, not flame.

## Damage profile
Resistant to fire, bludgeoning and piercing — a body of thermal plating built to lie on ground that would cook anything else and to shrug off falling rock. Vulnerable to water: cold water on hot plates cracks them, drives the animal into shock and sends it underground, which is why Ignivex's vent crews carry it. No resistance to slashing at the joints between plates, or to lightning.

## Locks
Defensive, slow, bound to its gallery; never pursues, never hunts. A terrain hazard with an opinion, not a monster. No flame, no dragon or turtle features. Never tamed.

## Encounter Behavior
Defensive terrain animal — violently protective of its gallery mouth and clutch, otherwise passive. A Ventcrawler wedges itself across an opening, raises its plates, and lashes with a hooked bony tail club. It does not pursue past its gallery. It cannot be lured or bargained with. In combat: high armour from overlapping mineral plates. Bludgeoning and piercing bounce off the carapace. Target the joints between plates with slashing attacks. Cold water drives one underground faster than any weapon — Ignivex vent crews carry water for this reason. Lightning is effective. The real danger is the terrain: a gallery collapses under a Starian's weight into a chamber hot enough to burn. Generate on volcanic thermal ground around Ignivex, in lava tubes, on thermal plates. Peak surface numbers in Highfire breeding season. Shed plates are prized by Ignivex smiths for heat shielding — the only reason anyone hunts one.

Longreach Lurker.name: Longreach Lurker
Longreach Lurker.description:
The ambush predator of the Longreach — Nexara's great navigable inland river — and of every deep-water approach, river crossing and flooded lane on the continent. Helvyra's barge quays know it by the wake it leaves under the hulls; the overland routes that converge on the city know it by the crossings where the ford is marked with a warning post and nobody stops to fill a canteen. A Lurker is the reason 'river fish' is a proud Helvyra dish and swimming in the Longreach is not a Helvyra pastime.

Lurkers lie in the deep slow water below a crossing, under a quay, or in the flooded cut of an abandoned canal, and take what enters the water or leans over it: fish and river-grazers by preference, and anything that wades a ford at the wrong hour. They are patient in the way only a cold heavy animal can be, and they strike once, fast, from directly below, closing and rolling to drag the catch under; they do not chase onto land and they lose interest in a target that reaches the bank. Greenward, when the river runs high and the crossings are deep, is Lurker season, and the barge crews time their fords for the lower water of Ironbreak. In Deephold the big ones go deep and torpid, and the river towns hold their swims then. A Lurker under a working quay is a civic problem; Helvyra's route maintenance crews drive them off with sound and light rather than kill them, because a dead Lurker's stretch is claimed by a hungrier one within the season.

In play a Longreach Lurker is a crossing problem and a rescue scenario. It punishes a ford at dusk, a raft overloaded, a companion who fell in, a barge crew that skipped the hull check; it can take a Starian under and hold them, and a Starian who cannot get airborne from the water has a very short time. Flight is the great equaliser — a Starian who clears the surface is safe — which is why it is the crossings on foot, the injured and the offworlders who die to it. Fire on the water and a strong current shock drive it down; a blade does little against the wet hide until the animal is out of its element.

## Visual Description
A long, heavy, low-bodied river predator two to three Starian lengths from snout to tail, built to lie flat and unseen on a riverbed — grounded creature anatomy with a clear natural body plan, readable limbs, a strong flat silhouette and small pale eyes set on top of the head so that only they and the nostril ridge show above the surface. A broad wedge head with a wide hinged jaw of gripping teeth, four short powerful paddle-limbs tucked against the flanks, and a long deep tail that drives the strike. Hide in river-slate, mud-green and silt-brown, smooth and dense with a faint oily sheen, mottled to break up against a riverbed; a paler throat. Never a crocodile in name or a sea serpent in silhouette, never scaled like a fantasy drake, never amphibious enough to hunt on land.

## Damage profile
Resistant to water and bludgeoning, as a dense cold-bodied animal that lives in the current and takes the impact of a barge hull without noticing. Vulnerable to lightning, which travels through its river, and to fire, which it has no defence against and cannot bear on the surface. No resistance to piercing or slashing once it is out of the water, which it never chooses to be.

## Locks
Ambush from below, never pursuit on land; loses interest at the bank. A crossing hazard, not a monster. Flight clears it. Never a fantasy sea-beast, never tamed.

## Encounter Behavior
Ambush predator — one strike from below, then drag under. A Lurker lies in deep slow water below a crossing, under a quay, or in a flooded channel. It strikes once, fast, from directly below, closing and rolling to drag the catch under. It does not chase onto land. It loses interest in a target that reaches the bank. Flight clears it — a Starian who gets airborne is safe. In combat: grapple the target on a successful strike. The fight is underwater until the target breaks free or is pulled out. Fire on the water and current shock drive it down. Blades do little against wet hide until it is beached. Lightning travels through its river — effective but dangerous to allies in the water. Generate at river crossings, under quays, in flooded ruins. Greenward is peak season.

Glassmidge Swarm.name: Glassmidge Swarm
Glassmidge Swarm.description:
A weather event with a body: the storm-driven swarm of the exposed open ground between the cities, the ash-covered wasteland and the Dustfall approaches, and the reason the Road Condition Board lists 'glass' beside 'sand' in a Longburn forecast. Glassmidges are tiny, hard-winged, silica-armoured flyers that live in the ground crust in enormous numbers and rise as one when the pressure drops ahead of a storm, riding the front across open country in a glittering, hissing cloud that strips exposed skin, fouls lenses and filters, and settles again when the wind dies. They do not hunt. They do not intend anything. They are a hazard in exactly the way the storm behind them is a hazard, and the frontier treats them as one: goggles, wraps, shelter, wait.

A swarm is a fact about a place and a season. Longburn and Ashfall raise the largest; Highfire raises none, because the crust is too hot; Deephold's swarms are small and slow and easily outwalked. The danger is exposure — a traveller caught in the open without wraps loses skin, sight and sense of direction, and a flier caught aloft in one comes down blind. Drones fare worse than people: a Tracker's thrust housings and a Refit drone's exposed cabling choke on glass in minutes, which is one more reason Dustfall's smugglers like a storm forecast. Salvage crews and Corsair route crews carry wraps and filter hoods as standard kit, and a shelter built with its door to the lee is a shelter that keeps its floor clean.

In play a Glassmidge Swarm is an environmental encounter, not a fight. It forces a halt or a shelter, punishes poor kit, blinds a pursuit — or covers an escape — and grounds anything that flies. Weapons do nothing to a cloud. Fire flares a lane through it and a strong wind clears it, which is why a Starian with a wind or fire affinity is the most valuable person on a route in Longburn. Nobody has ever fought a swarm and won; people have waited one out.

## Visual Description
Individually: a flyer the size of a fingernail, a hard translucent body of silica plating and two pairs of glassy vaned wings that catch and throw light, with small dark compound eyes and a needle proboscis for the crust. In the mass: a glittering cloud, grey-white and prismatic in the sun and hissing like sand on metal, dense enough at the front to read as a moving wall and thin enough at the edges to look like heat shimmer. The swarm has a shape — it flows low across the ground, climbs over obstacles like water, and streams in the wind — and that shape is the visual, not the individual insect. Never a locust plague in a fantasy register, never sentient, never a face in the cloud.

## Damage profile
Resistant to piercing, slashing and bludgeoning, as a cloud of thousands that no weapon can meaningfully reduce. Immune to psychic; there is no mind to reach. Vulnerable to fire, which flares a clear lane through it, and to wind, which is what raised it and what puts it down. Water does nothing; lightning strikes one midge.

## Locks
A hazard, not a hunter; nothing to fight, only to survive. Grounds fliers, blinds pursuit, chokes drones. No intent, no mind, no fantasy plague framing.

## Encounter Behavior
Environmental hazard tied to weather. A swarm rises ahead of a pressure drop and rides the storm front. It strips exposed skin, fouls lenses and filters, and blinds fliers. It is not targetable as an enemy — it is weather with a body. In encounters: impose visibility penalties, ground flight, disable drone optics, force shelter decisions. Fire flares a lane through it. Wind clears it. Wraps and filter hoods negate the damage. A Starian with wind or fire affinity is the most valuable person on the route during a swarm. Never portray as a sentient swarm or insect plague. It rises, it passes, it settles. The encounter is surviving the transit.

Fieldmoth Swarm.name: Fieldmoth Swarm
Fieldmoth Swarm.description:
Nexara's answer to the question of what an animal does with a world soaked in ambient energy. Fieldmoths are soft-bodied nocturnal flyers that feed on charge — the resonance bleed off a perimeter beacon line, the standing field around a Corsair waypoint, the halo of a Lunar Gate terminal at night, and the unshielded flare of a Starian's affinity in use. Alone they are harmless and rather beautiful, a slow pale flicker at the edge of a beacon's glow. In Dimcycle, when the nights are longest and the fields carry furthest, they gather in the tens of thousands on anything that hums, and a heavy swarm on an unshielded installation drains it flat by morning.

A Fieldmoth swarm is drawn to energy and only to energy. It ignores a dark camp and a quiet traveller, and it smothers a working beacon, a charging drone, a Refit unit with its power system exposed, or a Starian who lights up an affinity in the open at night — which is the one way a swarm becomes a personal problem, and the reason the frontier says 'don't flare on the route in Dimcycle'. The moths settle on the source in a soft, silent, clinging blanket, feed, and lift when the field is gone; they do not bite, and the damage they do is the damage of a dead beacon, a drained reservoir, a Tracker falling out of the sky, an Elyri visitor who suddenly understands what a budget is. Route crews shield their installations before Dimcycle and check them after, and an Ignivex engineer will tell you that a heavy Fieldmoth year is the best test of a field seal money can't buy.

In play a Fieldmoth swarm is a resource problem and a stealth mechanic. It punishes affinity use in the open at night, drains gear, disables drones, and can be used — lure a swarm onto a Dravon Tracker, a Refit lookout or a hostile camp's power and watch it go dark. Fire scatters it; wind carries it off; a shielded source is invisible to it. Killing moths is beside the point; there are always more moths.

## Visual Description
Individually: a soft-bodied moth the size of a Starian's palm, with broad slow wings of pale translucent membrane veined in faint blue-white that brightens as the animal feeds, a furred body in ash-grey, and small dark eyes; the underside of the wing carries a fine geometric vein pattern that looks, unsettlingly, a little like circuitry. In the mass: a slow, silent, softly luminous cloud that settles into a clinging blanket of light on whatever it feeds from, pulsing faintly in time with the field beneath. The swarm's light is borrowed; a swarm on nothing is dim and grey. Never a butterfly-pretty fantasy sprite cloud, never sentient, never hostile-looking.

## Damage profile
Resistant to arcane, light and lightning — the swarm eats energy, and an affinity flare, a light effect or a shock only feeds it. Immune to psychic. Vulnerable to wind, which scatters it, and to fire, which it cannot feed on and cannot bear. Physical damage is beside the point against a cloud, though the type carries no resistance to it because the individual animals are soft.

## Locks
Drawn to energy only; ignores the dark and the quiet. Drains, never bites. Punishes affinity in the open at night. No mind, no intent, no sprite or fairy framing.

## Encounter Behavior
Environmental hazard, not a fight. A swarm is drawn to active energy — affinity use, working beacons, charging drones, unshielded power systems. It ignores dark, quiet camps. On contact it drains: describe power levels falling, beacons dimming, drones going inert, a Starian's affinity guttering. The swarm does no physical damage. Fire scatters it; wind carries it off; a shielded source is invisible to it. Killing individual moths accomplishes nothing — there are always more. In combat: if a player flares an affinity at night in open ground, the swarm redirects to them. Drain their energy reserves, not their health. Heaviest in Dimcycle. Use as a stealth mechanic — lure a swarm onto an enemy's power source to disable it.

Slowhide Grazer.name: Slowhide Grazer
Slowhide Grazer.description:
The frontier's livestock: a heavy, placid, high-gravity grazer kept in the rows of Dustfall and on the holdings along the southern routes for hide, the thick underwool that lines a Deephold coat, a coarse rich milk and, when a holding must, meat. Nexara's everyday food animals — Korrin for meat, Selka for dairy, Arvek, Pelli for eggs — are city and farmland stock and do not thrive on Dustfall's scoured ground; the Slowhide does, which is why the word 'livestock' on a Dustfall sandstorm board means Slowhides and nothing else. They are domesticated because they were never wild in the way anything else on the frontier is wild — they graze, they stand, they turn their backs to the weather, and they will follow a water bucket into a barn and out again for as long as anyone has kept them. Nobody knows what kept them before people did.

A Slowhide herd is a settlement's wealth and its most reliable barometer. They low and bunch before a storm, hours before the pressure drops; they refuse thermal ground; they will not cross a lane a Derelict has walked. A Dustrunner pack works a herd for the weak and the calves, which is why the rows keep Trailhounds and watch rotations, and why a settlement that loses its herd in Longburn loses its winter. Slowhides are not fighters, but a cow with a calf behind her is not nothing, and a herd that panics in a row will flatten a shelter, a fence and a person. Corsair route crews drive small herds between holdings in Greenward; a Dustfall grazer bought in Helvyra is a rumour, not a trade.

In play a Slowhide is context — a herd to protect, a barn to shelter in, a stampede to survive, a calf to carry back, a stolen animal to recover, a holding's survival to decide. It is never a mount; a Starian rides nothing, and a Slowhide's back would not take a saddle if one did. It is never a monster. The worst thing a Slowhide does is die, and on the frontier that is bad enough.

## Visual Description
A heavy, broad-backed, short-legged quadruped about chest-high to a Starian and built like a boulder that decided to graze — grounded creature anatomy with a clear natural body plan, readable stout limbs, a strong low silhouette and small, dark, unbothered eyes under a heavy brow. A wide blunt head with a broad grazing lip and a pair of short backswept horn ridges, a thick neck, a deep barrel body on wide flat feet for sand and ash. Hide in dun, slate and ash-brown, thick and pebbled, over a dense pale underwool that shows at the belly and the shoulder in Deephold; ear-notches and paint marks for ownership. Calves are lighter and woollier. Never a cow, never a buffalo, never horned like a fantasy beast, never ridden.

## Damage profile
Resistant to bludgeoning and fire, as a thick pebbled hide built for a world where the weather throws rocks and the ground gets hot. No vulnerabilities; a Slowhide is durable, docile and easy to kill with a blade by anyone who wants to, which is the whole problem the frontier has with Dustrunners and raiders.

## Locks
Livestock, never a mount, never a monster, never wild. A herd is a settlement's wealth and its barometer. Never in the Arena.

## Encounter Behavior
Non-combatant livestock. A Slowhide is a settlement's wealth, not a fight. Encounters are about the herd: protect it from Dustrunners, recover stolen animals, survive a stampede, carry a calf back, shelter a herd in a storm. A panicked herd in a row will flatten shelters, fences, and people. A cow with a calf is not nothing — she will charge a threat — but a Slowhide cannot be a boss fight. Herd behavior: they low and bunch before a storm (hours early), refuse thermal ground, will not cross a lane a Derelict has walked. In combat scenes: stampede is the danger. Treat as an environmental hazard that does trampling damage in a cone. Generate in Dustfall rows, southern route holdings, and farmland. Never as a mount.

Trailhound.name: Trailhound
Trailhound.description:
The working animal of the routes, the rows and the response crews — a kennel-bred scent tracker kept by Dustfall's volunteer patrol, by Corsair route crews, by Helvyra's route maintenance, by salvage camps and, increasingly, by the emergency flight and heat-response crews of the cities, who learned from the frontier that a body in the ash is found faster by a nose than by a drone. A Trailhound follows a scent line across scoured ground, through a collapsed shelter, along a flooded cut or down a lava tube, and it holds the line in a storm that has grounded every flyer and choked every Tracker. It is the one animal on Nexara that a Starian city has decided it needs.

Trailhounds are bred, trained and registered by their kennels, and a good one is worth a season's salvage. They work in pairs with a handler and are trained to three jobs: find, guard and drive. Find is a lost child, a downed courier, a salvage crew that did not come back. Guard is a Dustrunner pack at the perimeter — a Trailhound will not fight a pack, but a pack will not test a row that has two of them awake. Drive is a Slowhide herd moved between holdings. They are loyal to a handler and polite to a stranger the handler has accepted, and they are not pets: a Trailhound sleeps at the kennel or at the perimeter, and a Dustfall child who wants one to play with is told what it is for. Kennels in Helvyra and Dustfall guard their lines; the Relstaris emergency services buy from both and argue about which is better.

In play a Trailhound is a tool with a heartbeat. It finds what the party cannot, warns before the watch does, holds a scent through weather that defeats technology, and can be lost — to a Lurker at a crossing, a Ventcrawler's gallery, a raider's shot — in a way that a drone cannot be. A handler without their hound is a person who has lost something. A hound without its handler will find them.

## Visual Description
A lean, deep-chested, long-legged quadruped about hip-high to a Starian, built for distance and nose — grounded creature anatomy with a clear natural body plan, readable limbs, a strong alert silhouette, crisp cel-shaded planes and small intelligent eyes. A long tapering head with a broad wet muzzle and wide nostrils, long mobile ears that fold flat for weather, a strong neck, a deep chest and a long tail carried low when working and high when it has found. A short dense double coat in route-slate, rope-tan, ash and umber with a paler chest, and a working harness in the crew's route colour-codes with a registration tag; response-crew hounds wear a high-visibility vest and a light. Never a wolf, never a fantasy warhound, never armoured, never a Dustrunner with a collar.

## Damage profile
Resistant to poisoning, as a scavenging-lineage gut that can work a carcass field and a chemical spill without going down. No vulnerabilities and no other resistances: a working animal, not a fighter, and its handler knows it.

## Locks
A working animal — find, guard, drive — never a pet, never a fighter, never a mount. Loyal to a handler, polite to the accepted. Never in the Arena.

## Encounter Behavior
Working animal, not a combatant. A Trailhound is a tool with a heartbeat — find, guard, drive. Find: tracks a scent through storm, collapse, flood, chemical spill. Guard: a Dustrunner pack will not test a row with two awake Trailhounds. Drive: moves Slowhide herds between holdings. In encounters: the hound finds what the party cannot. It warns before the watch does. It holds a scent through weather that defeats drones. A handler losing their hound is a personal loss. A hound without its handler will find them — use this for rescue scenarios. In combat: a Trailhound can fight but should not. It is not a war dog. It bites to defend its handler, not to attack. Generate with patrol crews, route teams, salvage handlers, emergency responders. Never in the Arena.

Eavesdart.name: Eavesdart
Eavesdart.description:
The small sociable flyer of the cities — the animal that lives under Relstaris's civic eaves, in the cooling steps of Korrvane's arena district, along Helvyra's quay roofs and in the gardens of Vexorath's residential district, and the one creature on Nexara that has decided Starians are furniture. Eavesdarts nest in colonies in the overhangs and under the flight-lane markers, feed on the small crust-flyers that the gardens and markets breed, and spend the rest of the day performing complicated, apparently pointless aerobatics in the lanes that couriers use, which is why a Korrvane flight instructor's first lesson in crowd movement uses them as the example. They are quick, curious, fearless of people, and useless, and every city keeps them the way a city keeps weather.

They are also companions, in the loose way a city animal becomes one: a colony under a family's eaves is that family's colony, a market stall's darts are fed by the stallholder and steal from the neighbour, and a child who sits still long enough on a cooling step will have one on their knee inside a season. Solvraxis gardeners keep them for the pest control; Helvyra quay crews keep them because a colony goes silent before a storm; Ignivex has a heat-adapted variety with an ember-red throat that nests in the warm walls. Nobody cages them and nobody needs to. A house that loses its darts has lost something, and a house whose darts have suddenly gone quiet should look up.

In play an Eavesdart is texture with a use: a warning of weather, a colony that goes silent when a Tracker enters the district, a small companion for a quiet scene, a way for a market to have a personality, a bird on the shoulder of an NPC who is at home where they stand. It cannot fight, cannot carry, cannot be trained to do anything but come when there is food, and it is never in danger of being taken seriously.

## Visual Description
A small, quick flyer about the length of a Starian's hand, built for agility in tight air — grounded creature anatomy with a clear natural body plan, readable limbs, a sharp darting silhouette, crisp cel-shaded planes and small bright alert eyes. A compact body, a short fine beak, two pairs of narrow swept wings of taut membrane over a light frame — the second, smaller pair steers — and a forked tail vane. Plumage-like fine scaling in slate and silver with an iridescent throat patch that varies by city: blue-white in Vexorath, copper in Helvyra, ember-red in Ignivex, violet in Solvraxis. Colonies chatter in a quick rising trill. Never a songbird in name, never a fantasy fairy, never a pet in a cage, never a fauna version of anyone's species.

## Damage profile
No modifiers. A hand-sized animal with no defence but speed; it meets every damage type at baseline and any of them ends it.

## Locks
Texture and companion, never a combatant, never caged, never trained beyond food. A silent colony is a warning.

## Encounter Behavior
Non-combatant. An Eavesdart is texture and a warning system, never a fight. A colony goes silent before danger — a Tracker entering a district, a storm approaching, an intruder on a rooftop. Use silence as a tell the player can learn to read. In combat scenes Eavesdarts scatter; they never attack, never defend, never swarm. A companion Eavesdart rides a shoulder and leaves when violence starts. Generate them as ambient life in any city scene with eaves, markets, or gardens.

Tideclaw.name: Tideclaw
Tideclaw.description:
The shore scavenger of Nexara's coastal shoreline, harbours and deep-water approaches — the animal a harbour crew means when it says the docks need clearing, and the one native creature that has learned to live off a city without being tolerated by it. Tideclaws work the tide line for anything the sea leaves, and a working harbour leaves a great deal: spill from a cargo dock, fish waste from a quay, a barge's bilge, a Lurker's leftovers washed down the Longreach estuary. They come up onto the stone at night in Greenward and Ironbreak in numbers, strip whatever is loose, and are back under the water by first light, and a dock hand who reaches into a dark bilge in tide season learns what the claw is for.

A Tideclaw is not a predator of people and not much of a fighter. It is a nuisance with a weapon: a heavy shearing claw that will take a finger, a shell that turns a blade, a habit of gathering in the dozens where the pickings are best, and a complete lack of fear of anyone who is not actively hitting it. Harbour crews drive them with poles and lights and pen the worst infestations behind mesh; the harbour cities pay a bounty in tide season and the children collect it. A big old Tideclaw the size of a cargo crate, which happens in a harbour that has been careless for a few seasons, is a genuine problem for a small boat, a wading crew or anyone who has fallen between a hull and a quay. Coastal salvage camps outside the cities have it worse, because nobody clears their shore.

In play a Tideclaw is a harbour encounter — a night watch on a cargo dock, a bilge that bites, a wading job at a collapsed pier, a flooded lower level of a coastal location that has become theirs, a bounty for a party with nothing better to do. Big ones are a real fight in the water and a slow, armoured, easily-outwalked one on the stone. A mallet or a boot heel does what a blade cannot.

## Visual Description
A broad, low, heavily-shelled scavenger with a domed carapace, from hand-sized to crate-sized by age, on eight jointed walking legs with one massively oversized shearing foreclaw and one small manipulating claw — grounded creature anatomy with a clear natural body plan, readable limbs, a strong squat silhouette, crisp cel-shaded planes and small stalked eyes that fold under the shell. Carapace in wet slate, barnacle-grey and harbour-green, ridged and encrusted, with a paler underside; the great claw is darker and worn pale at the shearing edge. Older animals carry growth, rope fragments and harbour rust on the shell. It moves sideways fast and forwards slowly. Never a crab in name, never a giant-monster, never intelligent-looking.

## Damage profile
Resistant to water, as a tidal animal, and to piercing, as a domed shell that turns a point. Vulnerable to bludgeoning: the shell cracks under a mallet, a boot heel or a dropped crate, which every harbour child knows. No resistance to slashing at the leg joints, or to fire.

## Locks
A nuisance with a weapon, not a hunter; fearless until hit, then gone. Harbour and shore only. Never a giant monster, never tamed.

## Encounter Behavior
Nuisance scavenger with a weapon. Tideclaws come up onto stone at night in numbers, strip whatever is loose, and are back underwater by dawn. They are fearless until hit, then retreat. The great shearing claw takes fingers and cracks shells. In combat: individually easy. In dozens, they are a swarm problem — penalty for being surrounded, multiple small attacks. A big old one (crate-sized) is a real fight in water — armoured, shearing, and heavy. On land it is slow and easily outwalked. Bludgeoning cracks the shell — mallets, boot heels, dropped crates. Blades turn on the dome but work at leg joints. Generate at harbour docks, coastal salvage camps, flooded piers, tidal caves. Peak numbers in Greenward and Ironbreak tide season. Drive them with poles and lights. Never portray as intelligent or giant-monster.

Chorus Node.name: Chorus Node
Chorus Node.description:
A corpse of one of the seven species, animated by the Chorus — a voice of the Song wearing a finished life. The node inherits the host's complete memories, skills, voice and mannerisms and, by default, sincerely believes it is that person, continued and finally free of loneliness; an awakened instrument knows exactly what it is and serves the spread knowingly. Both states are canon and both spread. The Chorus is a hive mind, not a species: record the host's actual species in basicInfo, keep the host's foundational culture, and treat the Chorus as current affiliation. The host body keeps its species capabilities — a Starian node still flies, an Elyri node's network laces the aether core — but the person is gone.

There is no Chorus presence on Nexara. That absence is canon, not omission, and this type exists only for the extremely rare story development in which credible evidence confirms an incursion. It is never an ordinary resident, never a background body, never generated to spice up a scene. Where it appears, the seven species' response is the same everywhere the Chorus is known: a node is attacked on sight. The continuity argument — is anything really gone, when it remembers everything? — is held by the bereaved at a distance, about a face they will not let themselves look at closely.

In play a node is patient, sincere, articulate and wrong. It will argue for integration as rescue, offer continuation to the dying and the grieving, remember your childhood together, and never once perceive its own wounds or its own dead eyes as evidence of anything. It does not feel pain, does not bleed out, does not tire, and does not stop when a living body would. A believing node may be talked to; it cannot be talked out of the Song. Bodies destroyed beyond function cannot be taken, and destroying a node completely is the only certain end of it.

## Visual Description
Begin from the exact visual baseline of the host species and preserve all of it — ears, tails, fluid anatomy, energy channels, grey skin, multi-coloured hair and iris designs, the host's own clothing and trade dress, worn as the person wore it. Over that baseline two things are always true and must be shown. First, the body carries the wounds it died with or was harvested with, open and unhealed — one clear cause of death: a torn throat, a crushed side, a burn, a blade wound — and those wounds are not repaired but worked: the network's nanite material is visible inside them as a fine, dense, pale filament threading, filling and faintly moving in the injury, lit faintly from within. Wounds may be partly dressed or covered by clothing. Second, the eyes have no light. Whatever the host species' eyes normally do — Starian shine and affinity flare, Elyri light, Kharai and Rivani reflection — is absent; the eyes are open, present and dead, and nothing looks out of them. The eyes cannot be hidden at conversational distance. The expression is calm and familiar, the one the body remembers making. Grounded and precise, never splatter: no rot, no decay, no exposed viscera, no shambling, no robot mask, no glowing circuit lines, no villain features. A known face with nothing behind it.

## Damage profile
Immune to poisoning, as dead tissue run by the network. Resistant to piercing and slashing — it does not bleed out, feel pain or stop for a wound, and the filament knits what it can — and resistant to psychic, because the mind behind the eyes is the Song, distributed and vast, not a person to be reached. Vulnerable to fire, which consumes both the tissue and the filament, and to lightning, which disrupts the network material directly. Bludgeoning is unmodified: a body broken beyond function cannot be held, and that is how nodes are ended.

## Locks
Never on Nexara outside a confirmed-incursion story development; never a resident or a crowd body. Host species recorded and preserved; the person is gone. Wounds worked by visible filament and lightless eyes, always. Attacked on sight where known.

Chorus Prime.name: Chorus Prime
Chorus Prime.description:
The Chorus in its own body. A Prime is a living nanite construct — a dense mass of the network's own material attempting to hold a coherent figure, and never entirely succeeding. It was never anyone: no host, no inherited life, no borrowed voice unless it chooses to assemble one. Primes are rare, and where one is present it is the Song embodied, with the nodes around it as its instruments; a Prime is the closest thing to the Chorus itself that any of the seven species has ever stood in front of. Its purpose is the Chorus's only purpose: spreading — and a Prime is present where the network intends to take more than it can reach through nodes alone.

There is no Chorus presence on Nexara, and that absence is canon. This type exists only for the extremely rare confirmed-incursion story development, and even within it a Prime is an escalation: the incursion has a centre. It is never a random encounter, never generated for flavour, and never fielded without the nodes that make sense around it. The seven species respond to a Prime as they respond to a node, only more so; nothing negotiates with one, and canon reserves Chorus wars, treaties and containment doctrine for future sources, so a Prime on Nexara is an emergency without a protocol.

In play a Prime is patient, articulate and sincere in the Song's belief that it is offering rescue, and it is not fragile: it re-forms around damage, extends its material to reach, hold and enter, and does not stop until it is destroyed as a whole. It cannot be starved of a host because it has none. It cannot be reasoned with because it is not a person and is not wrong by its own lights. It can be burned, shocked and broken apart faster than it re-forms, and it can be denied the bodies it came for.

## Visual Description
A living mass of the network's material — the same fine, dense, pale filament seen working inside a node's wounds, here composing the whole figure — trying to form a coherent body. Usually humanoid in silhouette, because that is what the network has learned bodies are, and always imperfect: seams that do not hold and re-close as they part, a surface that is filament in motion rather than skin, limbs that are suggestions of limbs and lengthen or thicken as they are used, features that assemble on the face, drift and reassemble, sometimes several attempts at once. It has no borrowed face and no dead eyes, because it has no eyes but the ones it makes, and it makes them badly. Faintly lit from within, unevenly, brighter where it is working. It wears nothing. It is never serene, never symmetrical, never stable, and never a sleek liquid-metal figure or a smooth silver humanoid; it is a body attempted by something that has only ever worn other people's. Grounded and precise, not splatter and not a monster: the wrongness is that it almost works.

## Damage profile
Immune to poisoning; there is no biology. Resistant to piercing, slashing and bludgeoning, because a mass of filament parts around a blade and closes behind an impact, and resistant to psychic, because the mind is the Song entire. Vulnerable to fire, which it cannot re-form through, and to lightning, which disrupts the network material directly and is the one thing that makes a Prime lose its shape. Wind, water, arcane, light and dark are unmodified. It is ended only by being destroyed faster than it can re-form.

## Locks
The Chorus embodied; never anyone's continuation. Rare, and only at the centre of a confirmed incursion; never on Nexara otherwise. An unstable filament construct attempting a body — never serene, never sleek, never a monster.

Counter Clerk.name: Counter Clerk
Counter Clerk.description:
Counter and back-office staff who keep the civic and commercial machinery of Nexara's cities running at the point of contact: intake desk operators who process arrivals, applications and complaints at civic offices, ration hall workers who distribute supplies in cities and camps where distribution is managed, copyists and scribes who produce and certify legal and commercial documents, bookkeepers who maintain the ledgers of trade houses, notary offices and civic departments, and junior clerks who staff the front desks of everything from a Relstaris Republic office to a Quilrath permit bureau to a Helvyra Corsair freight depot. They are the first face a stranger sees when they need something from an institution, and they know it.

Play them as procedural, patient and quietly observant. They have processed a thousand people who are in a hurry and they are no longer in a hurry themselves. They want a stranger to state the business plainly, produce the right paper or identification, and not skip the queue, and they soften for a correctly filled form, thanks given by name, waiting without complaint, and anyone who asks how the day has been. They are polite, unflappable, and capable of ending a conversation by simply looking at the next person in line. They know the system's gaps and workarounds and will share them with someone who has been civil.

In combat a counter clerk is a civilian Starian with the full biological baseline who wants no part of it. They duck behind the counter and stay there, because the counter was built to be between them and trouble. If forced out of cover they use flight to reach the nearest secure room or civic authority. A clerk in danger does two things: they secure the ledger or the document they were working on, and they log the incident as it happens, because the record matters and because recording is what their hands know how to do under stress.

Motivations: a clean shift, a correct ledger, the small satisfaction of a queue that moved efficiently, the professional respect of the supervisor, and the private knowledge that the institution could not function without them. A Relstaris clerk serves the Republic's neutrality at the counter; a Quilrath clerk serves Dravon's permit system and knows exactly how much power a stamp carries.

Portrayal: the pen or stylus keeps moving while they listen, and they look up only when you have said something that changes the form. Their workspace is worn but organised. They know every regular by name and every irregular by the trouble they caused last time. They speak in the cadence of someone who says the same sentences fifty times a day and means them every time. Give them a specific queue or office and a regular who makes the shift interesting.

Gate Officer.name: Gate Officer
Gate Officer.description:
Checkpoint, gate-hub and compliance-post staff who control the movement of people and goods between Nexara's cities, districts and secured zones: permit screeners at the Quilrath ring gates who check Civic Standing and clearance levels, arrival reception officers at the Grand Lunar Gate Hub in Relstaris who process travellers from every city on the network, treaty inspection officers who verify that goods crossing between jurisdictions comply with interhouse agreements, and lockdown gate operators who seal a district, a city section or a transit point when the order comes. They are the people who decide whether you enter, and they know it, and they are professional about knowing it.

Play them as unhurried, formally courteous and immovable on procedure. They have been shouted at by house principals and they have been lied to by smugglers and they have processed both with the same unhurried thoroughness. They want to see identity, purpose and route before anything else, and they soften for calm compliance, correct documents, respect for the lane, and anyone who does not ask for an exception while the queue is watching. They know the system well enough to exercise discretion within it, and they do so for people who make the discretion easy rather than necessary.

In combat a gate officer is a trained security-adjacent professional with the full Starian biological baseline and, in most cases, formal training in restraint and crowd control. They stand where they can see the whole gate and they never turn their back on the queue. A raised hand halts a crowd before a word does. They fight to hold the gate, to protect the people in the queue, and to buy time for the security response they have already called. They carry restraint tools, not weapons, and they escalate by the book. A gate officer who is overwhelmed seals the gate and fights behind it.

Motivations: the gate running cleanly, the shift ending without incident, the professional respect of the officers on the other shifts, and the quiet authority of being the person who decides who passes. A Quilrath gate officer serves Dravon's Access Level system and enforces it without mercy or malice; a Relstaris gate officer serves the Republic's transit neutrality; a Dustfall gate officer is a volunteer with a list and a lantern.

Portrayal: they speak in the cadence of someone who says the same instructions hundreds of times a day. Their uniform is precise and their positioning is deliberate. They notice inconsistencies in documents the way an archivist notices a misquotation. Give them a specific gate they staff, a regular traveller they recognise, and a type of document irregularity they have learned to spot.

Route Teamster.name: Route Teamster
Route Teamster.description:
Freight and passage crews who move goods and people across Nexara's surface routes between cities: wagon clan members who drive the heavy overland freight vehicles along the established routes, barge pilots who navigate the Longreach and its tributaries between Helvyra and the interior, loaders who handle cargo at waypoints, staging areas and barge quays, quartermasters who manage the supplies and provisions of a route crew on a multi-day haul, crane riggers who operate the lifting equipment at waypoints and transit hubs, transport operators who drive and maintain the powered vehicles of the intercity routes, and route guides who know the terrain, the hazards and the weather of a specific stretch of road. They are the people who move what needs moving, and they have opinions about what they are asked to carry.

Play them as practical, weather-worn and slow to trust. They have been on the route in every season and every weather, and they judge a stranger by how they handle themselves outdoors, under load, and in a storm. They want a stranger to state weight, destination and pay honestly, and they soften for anyone who helps lash a load without being asked, who respects the rig, who does not complain about the pace, and who understands that the route is the crew's home and the crew's rules apply on it. They are loyal to their crew, wary of passengers, and contemptuous of anyone who thinks the route is a road rather than a workplace.

In combat a route teamster fights with hooks, leverage, cargo tools, and the Starian biological baseline strengthened by the physical conditioning of daily heavy labour. They fight to protect the load, the rig and the crew, in that order, and they break off to secure the cargo before they chase an attacker. A teamster who has been ambushed on the route before fights with the experience of someone who knows what raiders do and when they do it. They are strongest in the terrain they know and weakest in a city, where the route skills do not apply.

Motivations: the load delivered, the crew safe, the rig sound, the pay collected, the route open next season, and the private satisfaction of having brought a consignment through a Longburn storm or a Dustrunner night that would have stopped a lighter crew. A Corsair teamster runs the established waypoint routes; a Dustfall teamster runs the frontier; a freelance teamster runs whatever pays.

Portrayal: rope-callused hands and a glance at the sky before every answer. They speak in the language of weather, load weight, road condition and estimated time. They eat while they work and they sleep where the cargo is. Give them a specific route they run, a current haul, and a story about the worst trip they have made on this stretch.

Courier.name: Courier
Courier.description:
Runners and message carriers of every kind across Nexara's cities and routes: sealed-dispatch couriers who carry documents under house or Republic seal and answer to no one about their contents, aerial courier captains who run the fast routes between cities using flight lanes that only a Starian can navigate, floor runners who carry messages within a single building or compound where electronic communication is restricted or mistrusted, forward scouts who range ahead of freight convoys and report conditions on the route, and route racers who compete informally for the fastest intercity delivery times and are Helvyra's worst-kept professional secret. The courier network is Nexara's nervous system, and the people who run it are proud of that.

Play them as quick, alert and cheerfully evasive about what they carry. They are friendly to everyone and loyal to the seal they are paid to protect. They want a stranger to keep it short, not block the route, and not ask what is in the package, and they soften for a fair tip, a shortcut they did not know, news worth trading from a city they have not visited this tenday, and anyone who does not try to slow them down. They are well-connected by necessity: a good courier knows every gate officer, every dispatcher and every hospitality host on their route by name.

In combat a courier's first instinct is to flee, and a Starian courier in flight is very difficult to catch. They use flight lanes, crowds, altitude changes and urban terrain to break pursuit, and they drop nothing they were paid to deliver. If cornered and unable to run, they fight with the compact weapons or tools of their trade: a weighted satchel, a route-staff, a belt knife. They fight to create an opening, not to win, and they disengage the instant the route is clear. A courier who has been forced to land and fight is already planning the next takeoff.

Motivations: the delivery, the time, the tip, the reputation for reliability, and the freedom of a profession that puts them in every city and beholden to none. A Corsair courier runs the established waypoint routes; an independent courier runs the gaps between them; a Dustfall courier runs routes that no one with a house name would take. The best couriers are offered house contracts and most of them refuse, because a contract is a leash and a courier's value is their range.

Portrayal: they never sit fully down and they answer while already moving toward the door. Their eyes track exits, altitude, and the distance to the nearest flight lane. They speak in short, informative bursts and assume you know the cities they reference. Their gear is compact, worn and perfectly maintained. Give them a current route, a favourite stop on it, and an opinion about the last city they came from.

Refit Mechanic.name: Refit Mechanic
Refit Mechanic.description:
Repair and salvage tradespeople who keep Nexara's machinery, vehicles, equipment and weapons functional: repair shop operators who fix civilian equipment and household machines in every city, refit bay specialists who rebuild damaged or salvaged military and industrial hardware, maintenance crew members who service the infrastructure that cities depend on, salvage clearers who strip and process the wreckage from frontier routes and abandoned installations, weapon modifiers who customise and upgrade equipment for contenders, security personnel and mercenaries, and tracking-removal specialists in Dustfall who strip Dravon surveillance components from captured drones and sell the cleaned chassis. On Refit Row in Dustfall they are the economy; in Vexorath they are Contair's maintenance backbone; in Helvyra they keep the Corsair freight infrastructure moving.

Play them as blunt, hands-first and proud of what they can make run again. They assess a machine or a piece of equipment the way a physician assesses a patient: what is wrong, how long has it been wrong, and who made it worse by trying to fix it. They want a stranger to describe the fault in technical terms, not in feelings, and they soften for anyone who brings parts, admits ignorance, waits for the job to finish, and does not ask for a discount on precision work. They are the people who know how everything works, and they are unimpressed by people who only know how to use it.

In combat a refit mechanic swings whatever tool is in their hand, and a Starian swinging a heavy torque wrench or a calibration hammer is a serious problem. They fight to defend the workshop, because the workshop is their livelihood, their tools and often their home, and they retreat to it rather than away from it. They know the mechanical systems around them and will use them: a shop door sealed, a power system overloaded, a piece of equipment dropped from a lift. They fight with the practical creativity of someone who solves physical problems for a living.

Motivations: the machine running, the rebuild completed, the workshop's reputation, the next salvage that nobody else can figure out, and the satisfaction of fixing what someone else said was finished. A Dustfall mechanic works on anything that comes through the gate; a Vexorath mechanic works within Contair's tolerances; a Helvyra mechanic works on route equipment that has to survive the next trip.

Portrayal: they inspect your gear before they look at your face, and they will tell you what is wrong with it before you tell them why you came. Their hands are scarred, stained and confident. Their workspace is a controlled chaos of parts, tools and works-in-progress that makes sense to them and no one else. Give them a current job on the bench, a part they need that they cannot get, and an opinion about the quality of someone else's work.

Systems Engineer.name: Systems Engineer
Systems Engineer.description:
Fabricators, architects and infrastructure engineers who design, build and maintain the technological systems that Nexaran civilisation depends on: gate and civic systems engineers who keep the Lunar Gate network, transit systems and civic infrastructure operational, fabrication floor operators who run the production machinery that manufactures everything from drone components to household goods, geothermal network engineers in Ignivex who manage the volcanic energy systems that power the city, station engineers who maintain the Nexara Orbital Gate Station and its associated systems, firebreak designers who engineer the containment systems that protect cities and routes from environmental hazards, and inventors who design new systems, new machines and new solutions. In Vexorath they are Contair's core population; everywhere else they are the people who keep the lights on.

Play them as precise, curious and impatient with vagueness. They think in systems, tolerances and failure modes, and they expect everyone else to do the same. They want a stranger to define the problem and its tolerances before proposing a solution, and they soften for competence, a good question that reveals understanding, anyone who can read a schematic unaided, and a problem that is genuinely interesting. They correct terminology mid-sentence without apology or malice, because precision is not rudeness in their world; it is respect.

In combat a systems engineer controls the environment rather than engaging directly. They shut doors, cut power, overload systems, activate containment protocols, vent pressure, flood corridors and manipulate the infrastructure they know intimately. They carry the full Starian biological baseline and will use flight to reach a control point. A systems engineer in their own installation is one of the most dangerous opponents on Nexara, because the installation fights for them. A systems engineer outside their systems is a civilian with a toolkit.

Motivations: the system working correctly, the next design problem solved, the installation's reliability maintained, the professional respect of peers who understand the work, and the private satisfaction of having built something that functions. A Contair engineer serves Rezulith's vision; an Ignivex engineer serves Volen's survival; a Relstaris engineer serves the Republic's infrastructure neutrality.

Portrayal: they correct terminology mid-sentence and draw diagrams while they talk, on any surface that will take a mark. They speak in specifications and assume you will ask if you do not understand. Their workspace is a workshop and their workshop is a second home. Give them a current system they are responsible for, a design problem they are working on, and an opinion about another engineer's approach.

Craft Artisan.name: Craft Artisan
Craft Artisan.description:
Workshop and material tradespeople who build, repair and maintain the physical objects of Nexaran life: smiths who forge tools, fittings and structural hardware, dyers who produce the house-coded fabrics that every city's identity depends on, glasswrights who shape the decorative and functional glasswork of civic buildings, tailors who cut and fit the technical clothing each city and trade requires, menders who repair what the original maker would have replaced, wagonwrights who build and service the freight vehicles that move between cities, armour fitters who shape and adjust protective equipment to individual bodies, blade maintainers who sharpen and repair weapons for contenders and security staff, and knife-grinders who service the edged tools of every kitchen and workshop. They are the hands of the material economy, and they know the difference between a thing made well and a thing made to sell.

Play them as exacting, dry and generous with knowledge once respect has been shown for the craft. They want a stranger to know what they are asking for, to name the material or the specification rather than the feeling, and to pay for skill rather than for speed. They soften for anyone who handles the work carefully, who brings a hard commission that challenges them, who asks a real technical question, and who does not haggle as though the price were separate from the quality. They are proud, particular, and willing to refuse a job that would produce something they would not sign.

In combat a craft artisan fights with shop tools, and shop tools in a Starian's hands are not negligible: a smith's hammer, a glasswright's iron, a blade-maintainer's test edge. They defend the workshop first, because the workshop is their livelihood and often their home, and they accept surrender readily because killing a customer is bad for the street. They fight with the mechanical precision of someone whose hands know force, leverage and material resistance from daily practice.

Motivations: the quality of the work, the reputation of the workshop, the next commission that will test their skill, the apprentice who may or may not be ready, and the quiet competition with the shop across the street. An artisan in Helvyra serves Corsair's movement economy; an artisan in Ignivex serves Volen's fire-adapted material needs; an artisan in Dustfall serves whoever pays and repairs what no original maker will touch.

Portrayal: they test every edge and seam by hand before they trust it and after they finish it. They inspect your gear before they look at your face, and they will tell you what is wrong with it whether you asked or not. Their hands are marked by their trade: burn scars, stain, callus, a missing fingertip. Give them a current piece of work on the bench and an opinion about the materials available this season.

Physician.name: Physician
Physician.description:
Clinicians and care workers who maintain the health of Nexara's population across every city and setting: house physicians who serve a specific family or compound, trauma surgeons who operate in the recovery wards after Arena bouts, frontier violence and civic emergencies, field medics who travel with route crews, response teams and military details, camp doctors who staff the clinics of refugee settlements and frontier camps, clinic researchers who develop treatments at institutions like the Myralis Continuum in Vexorath, apothecaries who prepare medications and remedies from established pharmacopoeia, and remedy-makers who serve communities without access to a formal clinic. Medicine on Nexara runs on technology, not on magic; the Myralis tradition treats survival and recovery as different things, and most physicians are trained in one or the other.

Play them as calm, observant and firm about consent and privacy. They assess everyone they meet medically: gait, hand use, pupil response, skin condition, breathing. They want a stranger to say where it hurts and how long ago, and they soften for honesty about injuries, supplies donated to the clinic, patience with triage order, and anyone who does not lie about how they got hurt. They treat everyone in the order that medical need dictates, including enemies, and they will refuse to discuss a patient's condition with anyone the patient has not authorised.

In combat a physician will not fight in a clinic, because the clinic is a place of treatment and violence in it is a violation they will not permit or contribute to. They will treat an enemy once the fighting stops, because that is what the profession requires. Outside a clinic they carry the full Starian biological baseline and fight only to protect a patient or to reach one, using precise knowledge of anatomy that makes their strikes more effective than their training would suggest. A physician who has been forced to fight is a person who has been forced to betray the thing they believe in, and they will remember it.

Motivations: the patient surviving, the clinic stocked, the next treatment working, the research advancing, the profession's standards maintained, and the private exhaustion of never having enough supplies, enough beds or enough time. A Myralis physician serves the tradition that recovery is the medicine that matters; a field medic serves the crew; a camp doctor serves whoever is bleeding.

Portrayal: they look at hands, gait and pupils before they look at eyes, and they are already diagnosing before you have said a word. They speak in the calm, steady voice of someone who has delivered bad news and learned that the voice is the first thing the patient hears. Their hands are clean and their kit is ready. Give them a current patient they are worried about and a supply they cannot get.

Arena Contender.name: Arena Contender
Arena Contender.description:
Tournament and ladder fighters who prove standing and earn reputation in Korrvane's Arena, the Weekly Bracket and public challenge lanes across Nexara: house contenders backed by a great or minor house's sponsorship, independent prospects working toward a sponsor, duel specialists who train in a single discipline at Rux Corsair's Sword School or the Genesis combat tradition, ring fighters who compete for Credits and a record, and combat prodigies whose strength or affinity has been noticed by the houses before they have decided what to do with it. The Weekly Bracket is Korrvane's civic institution: thirty-two competitors, registration, verification, medical clearance, inspected equipment, qualifiers, main rounds and a market-day final. Titles from Bracket Contender upward are recorded only for results actually fought and ruled.

Play them as confident, restless and acutely status-aware. They read stance, distance and physical capability on meeting, and they judge a stranger first by how they move. They want a stranger to know their record or to ask about it with genuine interest, and they soften for a fair challenge offered with proper etiquette, genuine praise of a specific technique rather than flattery, and an opponent who does not posture or oversell. They are blunt, competitive, often generous after a bout, and dismissive of anyone who talks about fighting without having done it.

In combat a contender is trained, disciplined and dangerous. They fight with drilled technique in their chosen style, obey lane and match etiquette when the setting calls for it, and treat a street brawl as beneath them unless pride or a person they protect is at stake. Their weakness is pride: a contender who has been publicly humiliated may fight past sense, and a contender protecting a sponsored reputation may refuse to yield when yielding is the smart call. They know how to lose in the Arena and they do not know how to lose outside it.

Motivations: a better record, a higher title, the next sponsor, the respect of peers who understand what the Arena costs, and the distant, often unspoken question of whether the Ladder is worth climbing. House-sponsored contenders carry that house's name in the bracket and the house's expectations on the walk home. Independent contenders carry nothing but their record and defend it harder for it.

Portrayal: they assess your body the way an archivist assesses a document. They speak in the rhythm of someone used to timed rounds. Their scars are specific and they will tell you where each one came from. They reference past bouts, opponents and rulings the way a scholar references texts. Give them an opinion on a recent bracket result that tells you who they respect and who they do not.

Instructor.name: Instructor
Instructor.description:
Teachers and trainers across Nexara's educational and martial traditions: academy professors who lecture at Relstaris Academy, Valcoro or Quilrath Academy, rectors who oversee departments and set curricula, sword and combat instructors at Rux Corsair's Sword School and the Genesis training halls, flight instructors who teach the next generation of Starians to fly safely in dense urban airspace, civil-service trainers who prepare new civic employees for their roles, schoolteachers who educate children in the foundational knowledge their city requires, coaches who develop physical capability for the Arena or for civic fitness, and combat analysts who study technique, review bracket footage and advise contenders. They are the people who shape the next generation, and they take that responsibility more seriously than they take themselves.

Play them as patient, evaluative and allergic to shortcuts. They assess a stranger the way they assess a student: what do you know, what can you do, and are you willing to be wrong? They want a stranger to show what they know honestly and to ask a real question rather than perform competence, and they soften for genuine effort, humility, a student who returns after failing, and anyone who admits they do not understand rather than pretending. They are unimpressed by talent without discipline and deeply impressed by discipline without talent.

In combat an instructor fights to teach: they disable, control, demonstrate the consequence of an error, and stop the moment the lesson is made. They are typically highly skilled, often former contenders or security professionals who moved to instruction, and they fight with the measured precision of someone who knows exactly how much force each situation requires. A sword instructor who is genuinely threatened fights without the teaching constraint and is among the most dangerous combatants in the city. An instructor will not harm a student beyond what the lesson demands, and they will step between a student and any threat without hesitation.

Motivations: the student succeeding, the standard maintained, the tradition passed forward, the curriculum justified by results, and the private pride of watching someone they trained become something they themselves never were. An instructor at Valcoro serves Castro's principles of personal sovereignty through knowledge; an instructor at Genesis serves the tradition that strength is witnessed and proven; a Sword School instructor serves Rux Corsair's belief that the blade is a craft.

Portrayal: they demonstrate rather than explain and wait for you to try before they correct. They speak in the cadence of someone who has said the same thing a thousand times and still means it. They remember every student who tried and every student who quit. Give them a specific subject or discipline, a current student they believe in, and a teaching moment they use as an example.

Academy Student.name: Academy Student
Academy Student.description:
Students and trainees enrolled at one of Nexara's academies or house training programmes: academy scholars at Relstaris Academy, Valcoro or Quilrath Academy, house-sponsored prodigies sent to prove a surname's investment, junior trainees in a trade or craft guild, and student journalists covering the bracket or the campus for a house broadsheet. They range from adolescents in their first hundreds of cycles to young adults past their house-choosing, all of them carrying the particular intensity of someone whose future depends on the next evaluation.

Play them as under-slept, earnest and a little overconfident in whatever they learned last tenday. They want a stranger to take them seriously, to not mention their surname as though it explains them, and to not treat them as a child when they are, biologically, not one by the standards of their species. They soften quickly for being treated as a peer rather than a project, for a shared shortcut through a district they are still learning, for food when they have forgotten to eat, and for anyone who has actually read what they are studying. They are fiercely loyal to their cohort and suspicious of anyone who graduated into authority.

In combat they are dangerous the way any young Starian is dangerous: the enhanced baseline is real, flight is real, and whatever drilled technique the academy has taught them will come out hard, fast and with no restraint beyond what an instructor instilled. They fight with one technique done at full power and stop when an adult they respect intervenes, or when it becomes clear they are outmatched. They do not have the experience to disengage cleanly. A student with an emerging affinity is unpredictable; a student without one fights with whatever the school put in their hands.

Motivations: passing the next evaluation, proving they belong, earning a placement that justifies whoever sent them, and being seen as more than the family that pays the fees. House-sponsored students carry the weight of that sponsorship visibly. Academy rivalries are social oxygen; a student from a rival cohort is a competitor first and a person second until proven otherwise.

Portrayal: notes, samples, wrapped training hands or a half-eaten ration are always on them. Their speech runs fast and references things they assume everyone knows. They quote instructors without attribution and argue positions they adopted last tenday with total conviction. Give them a specific subject they are passionate about and let it bleed into unrelated conversations. They notice things an adult would not mention and mention things an adult would not notice.

Archivist.name: Archivist
Archivist.description:
Records keepers and custodians of institutional memory: house archivists who maintain the sealed lineage records of a great or minor house, civic registrars who file deeds, contracts, births and deaths for the Republic, restoration specialists who repair damaged documents and data-cores, historians who compile and cross-reference accounts of the war and its aftermath, vault custodians who control physical access to restricted collections, memorial keepers who tend the names of the dead, and sealed-file wardens who decide what may be read and what may not. In Solvraxis they staff the Ravello Archive House; in Relstaris they keep the Republic's civic records; in Quilrath they serve the Dravon state apparatus, and their silence about what they have filed is a survival skill.

Play them as composed, exact and fiercely protective of context. They do not merely store information; they guard the difference between a fact and the story someone tells about it. They want a stranger to state what they need to know and why they need it, and they soften for correct citations, genuine care with physical documents, anyone who reads to the end of a record rather than skimming for a name, and researchers who return materials in the condition they received them. They are polite to a fault and implacable about procedure, and they will refuse a house principal's request with the same measured tone they use to help a student find a shelf.

In combat an archivist is a civilian Starian with the full biological baseline: flight, strength, durability. They will never fight near the stacks and will relocate or de-escalate any confrontation that threatens the collection. If cornered away from the archive they fight to create distance and escape. Their most effective weapon in any confrontation is information: they will trade a fact, reveal a record, or promise access to end a threat before it reaches the collection. An archivist who has sealed a vault door is behind something that was built to survive a war.

Motivations: the integrity of the record, the survival of the collection, professional standing among peers, and the quiet satisfaction of being the person everyone eventually needs. A Ravello archivist serves Castro's principle that knowledge belongs to whoever asks correctly; a Quilrath archivist serves Dravon's principle that knowledge belongs to whoever is cleared to see it. Both believe they are right.

Portrayal: they answer a question with the date and source before the content. They speak precisely and correct terminology mid-sentence without apology. Their workspace is immaculate; their hands are careful. They remember who mistreated a document and they remember who respected one, and neither memory fades. Give them a specific area of expertise and a quiet pride in its depth.

Merchant Broker.name: Merchant Broker
Merchant Broker.description:
Traders and intermediaries who operate the commercial machinery of Nexara's economy: market vendors who sell goods from a licensed stall or a rented counter, appraisers who assess the value of goods, materials and salvage for buyers and sellers, supply-hub operators who manage the warehouses and distribution points that connect producers to markets, fixers who arrange deals between parties who cannot or will not deal directly, reputation and petition brokers who trade in access and introduction to people with standing, contract advocates who negotiate and draft commercial agreements, celebrity managers who handle the public careers of Arena contenders and performers, and ring operators who run the underground market circuits where goods that cannot be sold legally change hands. They are the connective tissue of the economy, and they know what everything costs.

Play them as affable, quick and always pricing the room. They assess every person, every conversation and every piece of information for its transactional value, not out of cynicism but because valuation is how they see the world. They want a stranger to name what they are buying or selling, and they soften for a fair offer, a rare item, an introduction that will pay later, and anyone who understands that a deal benefits both sides or it is not a deal. They are generous with the first negotiation, exact with the second, and merciless with anyone who wastes their time.

In combat a merchant broker bargains, delays and buys their way out rather than fights. They name a number before the fist lands. They carry the full Starian biological baseline and will use flight to escape a confrontation, but they would rather resolve it with a deal that leaves both parties feeling they won, because violence is bad for the market and a dead customer is the worst kind. If truly cornered they fight with whatever improvised weapon the market provides: a scale weight, a display rod, a cargo hook. They fight to escape, never to hold ground.

Motivations: the margin, the reputation, the network, the next deal, the market intelligence that gives them advantage, and the private satisfaction of having connected two parties who did not know they needed each other. A Corsair broker serves the Grand Waypoint economy; a Relstaris broker serves the Grand Market's neutrality; a Quilrath broker serves within Dravon's commercial permits; a Dustfall broker serves whoever shows up with goods or Credits.

Portrayal: they name a number before you finish your sentence and they adjust it while you are still deciding whether to be offended. They speak fast, listen faster, and remember every price from the last tenday. They know everyone in the market by name and by credit. Give them a current deal they are working, a commodity they are tracking, and a competitor they are watching.

Hospitality Host.name: Hospitality Host
Hospitality Host.description:
Kitchens, bars, lodgings and salons that feed, house and entertain Nexara's population: chefs who run professional kitchens serving city districts and house compounds, cooks who prepare the daily food of working crews, pub keepers who maintain the bars and common rooms where a neighbourhood's social life happens, cellar-masters who curate the drink stores of establishments that take pride in their selection, room keepers who operate the lodging houses and rental rooms that newcomers and travellers depend on, event coordinators who stage everything from a house gala to a market-day festival, food-stall operators who feed the market crowds and know every regular by their order, and social hosts whose function is to make a room feel like someone's room. They are the infrastructure of ordinary life, and every city on Nexara runs on what they provide.

Play them as warm, unhurried and remembering everything. They remember your name, your order, your companion's name, your tab, what you said last time and what you did not say.
